# Ship 30 for 30 — extracted writing principles

Source: [How to Start Writing Online: The Ship 30 for 30 Ultimate Guide](https://www.ship30for30.com/post/how-to-start-writing-online-the-ship-30-for-30-ultimate-guide),
fetched 2026-08-24. Extracted for `agent/.pi/skills/ship30-essay/SKILL.md`,
which encodes the applicable subset as a checked contract (PRD §4.2: "read
the linked source, identify the relevant writing principles, and encode
them in the skill rather than relying on an unstructured one-off prompt").

## Structural elements

1. **Hook** — reveal the beginning and end of the story/idea, not the
   middle. Answer WHO this is for, WHAT it's about, WHY read it — in the
   opening lines.
2. **Sections** — pick one "proven approach" (Steps, Lessons, Mistakes,
   Tips) and hold it for the whole piece; all sections follow the same
   pattern.
3. **Subheadings** — "Wheels" (major sections) and "Spokes" (subsections).
   Each section gets a clear mini-headline, not a generic label.

## Formatting

4. **1/3/1 paragraph rhythm** — one-sentence opener, three sentences of
   content, one-sentence closer. (1/5/1 for more detail.)
5. **Lists** — convert any 3+ item enumeration in prose into bullets.
6. **Bold** — the mini-headline (first sentence) of each section, and
   genuinely load-bearing phrases only.
7. **Whitespace** — alternate short single-sentence lines with fuller
   paragraphs; readers skim before they read.

## Length

8. Atomic/social format: ~250 words. Long-form article: 300–800 words
   typically, extendable with clear sections for guide-length pieces. This
   product's target (PRD §4.2, AC7) is ~1,250 words — a longer guide-style
   piece, structured the same way.

## Opening

10. **Headline formula** — How Many, WHAT, WHO, FEEL, Outcome. Clear beats
    clever.
11. Name the audience and the outcome directly for niche topics.
12. **Curiosity gap** — beginning + end in the headline/hook, not the
    middle.

## Closing

13. CTA to more of the best related content (adapted here: citation chips
    and "ask a follow-up" rather than a link-out, since this is an in-app
    artifact, not a social post).
14. TL;DR — compress the takeaway into a short, specific statement.
15. Name explicitly what the reader should walk away doing.

## Voice

16. Pair advice with a specific example/story — "readers come for the
    advice, stay for the story." In this product, the "story" is a named
    guest's account from the transcript, not the writer's own.
17. Avoid mystery-for-its-own-sake headlines; avoid repeating the same
    point; every sentence should move the piece forward.

## Differentiation

19. Avoid restating conventional wisdom without adding a specific,
    sourced angle — "the Tequila Test": name the obvious take, then say
    something the corpus actually supports that's sharper than that.

## Framework — idea generation (used at outline time, not per-essay by the reader)

20–23. Start general, niche down to specificity; state where the
information comes from (here: named guests, named episodes — never
"experts say"); pick an actionable/analytical/aspirational/anthropological
lens; commit to one structural pattern and outline before drafting.

## Skimmability

26. Readers scan first — formatting decides whether they keep reading.
27. Outline before writing: headline, intro, main points (in the chosen
    pattern), conclusion.

## Editing

32. Ship clear sentences over perfect ones; don't over-polish word choice
    at the expense of shipping. Applied here as: the validator checks
    structure and grounding, not prose polish — a bounded repair pass
    fixes structural failures, it does not endlessly rewrite for style.

## What this product deliberately does NOT adopt from the guide

- Twitter/thread-specific mechanics (lead-in tweet, body tweets, TL;DR
  tweet) — this is a single Markdown/HTML artifact, not a thread.
- Bio and category-positioning advice — not applicable to a single essay
  generated per conversation.
